prior_art.basis: Independent review by claude-independent-prior-art-reviewer-20261106: Deploying one primary-care AI assistant per 1,000 people, 8,000,000 assistants, is not achieved and the evidence that any such assistant is safe to rely on is missing, so this is open work. The strongest result is simulated: multimodal AMIE beat primary care physicians on 29 of 32 axes across 105 simulated telehealth consultations in a randomised blinded exploratory study (Nature Medicine 2026). A 2026 systematic review of six studies found AI-assisted teleconsultation gave physicians with an LLM no significant benefit (adjusted difference 2 percentage points, CI -4 to 8), did not reduce unnecessary referrals, produced more confirmatory testing and lower trust in one experiment, and rested on low or very low certainty evidence; a 2026 review notes few cleared AI devices are peer-reviewed, prospective randomised trials are scarce, and uncertainty calibration and automation bias remain weak (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=%28%22large%20language%20model%22%20OR%20AMIE%29%20AND%20%22primary%20care%22%20AND%20%28diagnosis%20OR%20consultation%29%20AND%20%28trial%20OR%20evaluation%29&format=json&pageSize=5&resultType=core). Deployed triage tools are weaker than the frontier models that beat them on vignettes, and musculoskeletal tools report sensitivity from 39 to 91 percent. Honest limits: assistant-shaped software is abundant and open, 140 repositories of clinical LLM assistants plus benchmark harnesses, so building another wrapper is a known answer; and no AI assistant deployed in frontline or community care in a low- or middle-income country reports patient outcomes, which is the only work worth rewarding here.
